They argue that methods like cropping, warping, and noise injection, while effective in other time series analysis tasks, disrupt the inherent temporal dependencies necessary for accurate forecasting. To address this, FrAug employs two distinct augmentation strategies: frequency masking, which involves randomly masking segments of the frequency representation of the time series, and frequency mixing, which combines frequency components from different time series. These operations are designed to preserve the semantic consistency of the augmented data-label pairs, ensuring that the frequency components in the labels (look-back window and forecasting horizon) remain aligned with their corresponding time series segments. This is especially pronounced in scenarios with distribution shifts, where FrAug helps models adapt more quickly to new data patterns. The paper also explores the effectiveness of FrAug in test-time training, where the model is periodically retrained on new data, demonstrating its ability to mitigate performance degradation over time.
